mappings.note: Asks for Porifera's highest level of organisation and the answer is 'cellular level' -- the exact phrase LO-6 uses for Porifera. Not C4.2-LO-5, the general phylum-placement row: the phylum is given and what is probed is the level itself, which is LO-6's business.

A complete gut with two openings marks the step from Platyhelminthes to the organ-system level -- LO-5 traces cells to tissues to organs to organ systems and uses the level reached to place the animal. Not LO-6: neither organism here is a sponge or a cnidarian.

Hydra's tentacles against the sedentary sponge is exactly LO-6's contrast between the tissue level in Cnidaria and the cellular level in Porifera, with the functional consequence (active capture rather than filtering) that the outcome implies.

Three candidate features of Platyhelminthes judged true or false, the discriminating one being the absence of a true body cavity -- body organisation used to characterise a phylum, LO-5. Platyhelminthes has no outcome of its own, unlike Cnidaria, Annelida and Mollusca.

Which phylum FIRST reaches the organ-system level with a two-opening gut: Nematoda. Same row as the Organism A/B item above and honestly so -- both turn on the same step in LO-5's ladder, and Nematoda has no row of its own to move one of them to.

A four-row plant table read for differentiation of root/stem/leaf and presence of vascular tissue -- body organisation, so the C4.2 competency that houses the plant divisions. Not C4.2-LO-5, which is explicitly about ANIMALS; this curriculum offers nothing closer for plants.

The reason clause is the whole item: the exoskeleton protects and limits water loss, therefore the group succeeded on land. That is adaptive structure and function, C4.5. Not C4.2-LO-5: the phylum is named in the stem, nothing is being placed.

The chapter's Mollusca placement item, so LO-8, the one Mollusca row. Recorded with a caveat: the item identifies the phylum from head, muscular foot, visceral hump and shell, whereas LO-8 is worded narrowly as 'the organ-system level of organisation in Mollusca and names the organ systems present' -- the external body plan the item actually uses is not what the outcome describes.

Four phylum-to-feature pairs checked for the correct one, Echinodermata with its calcium carbonate endoskeleton. LO-5 as the general placement row; Echinodermata, like Arthropoda and Chordata, has no outcome of its own.

Jointed appendages and distinct body regions separate the arthropod specimen from the annelid one -- placement from body plan, LO-5. Deliberately NOT the same code as the arthropod assertion-reason item, which asks the adaptive value of the exoskeleton and so sits on C4.5.

Vertebral column, internal skeleton and complex organ systems as the marks of vertebrates -- the top of LO-5's ladder used to place an animal. Not C4.5: the item lists defining features, it does not argue how they evolved.

POOR FIT: what happens to shared features as one moves Kingdom to Species belongs to the seven-rank hierarchy, which has no outcome in curriculum 82. C-4.1-LO-2 is cited for 'Classify various organisms in groups' alone; its named basis, cellular organisation and ecological role, is irrelevant here.

Four candidate RULES of binomial nomenclature -- two parts, capitalised genus, italics -- plus the universality claim, which is LO-3's 'significance and rules' in one item. Not C-4.1-LO-4: no organism is actually named, the rules themselves are the object.

POOR FIT, same gap as the Kingdom-to-Species item: this is the hierarchy read off a diagram rather than from words, and curriculum 82 has no rank-hierarchy outcome. Recorded as a duplicate rather than split artificially from its sibling.

Woese's three domains, proposed on genetic evidence, with Monera as the superseded term -- C7.1 for the current understanding that replaced the five-kingdom top level, LO-9 for the succession of kingdom systems it continues. Not C4.5: the evidence is used to reclassify, not to argue descent.

Simpler fossils in deeper layers, read as a record of life becoming more complex -- C4.5's 'evidences of biological evolution'. The only row in this curriculum that mentions evolution at all, and no learning outcome sits under it.

A four-animal table keyed on symmetry and level of organisation, resolved to the organ-level flatworm, plus the functional reason (diffusion across a flattened body). Placement from level of organisation, LO-5.

The consequence of removing one species is borne by the species that depend on it -- LO-15, 'interactions between members of different groups of organisms'. Held to this one code: unlike the ecosystem-stability item in part 1, this one never rises to the system scale that would justify adding C2.8.

Naming the term for the total variety of life from microscopic algae to giant trees -- the biosphere, C2.8. Same home as the other biodiversity-definition item; not C5.2, since nothing is asked about protecting any of it.

POOR FIT and the third of the rank-hierarchy items: two animals sharing an Order share more than two sharing only a Class. The genera in the table are decoration, so not C-4.1-LO-4 either -- the reasoning is entirely about rank depth, which this curriculum does not cover.

The Purple Frog discovery used to argue conservation urgency for a named region -- a case study about human choices, C5.2, whose examples include conservation of biodiversity. Not C2.8: the Western Ghats appears here as a threatened place, not as an ecosystem being described.

The ask is the local name of a habitat type -- phumdis, floating mats of vegetation -- so an ecosystem fact, C2.8. The endangerment in the stem is framing; the Loktak case-study item that actually asks about threats and conservation is mapped to C5.2 instead.

Why a universal system helps scientists communicate -- the 'significance' half of C-4.1-LO-3, and the model answer argues it entirely through binomial nomenclature and the failure of common names. Not C-4.1-LO-2: no organism is grouped anywhere in the item.

Binomial names APPLIED to four real animals: shared first word means shared genus, so Panthera uncia and Panthera tigris are the close pair. That application is LO-4, as against LO-3, which covers the rules in the abstract.

Mangroves against cyclones and soil microbes against pollutants are C2.8's Earth processes and hazards; the middle statement, diverse wildlife diluting tick-borne disease, is an interaction between groups of organisms, LO-15. Both earn their place because the three statements are scored separately.
